summary: Describes how to use CBC-mode cipher algorithms with IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload, both for specific ciphers and in general. It gives a common framework so many ciphers can be plugged in. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It shows how to plug in lots of different secret codes of the same style into the IPsec lock, using one set of instructions.

subtitle: One common recipe for using block ciphers such as Blowfish, CAST-128, IDEA, RC5 and 3DES with IPsec ESP.

tldr.problem: Each CBC-mode cipher used with the IPsec ESP protocol had its own document, even though they share the same mode, key size, weak key, block size and rounds questions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2451 merges these into one description. It fixes CBC mode, 8-octet blocks, keys in multiples of 8 bits, per-cipher defaults, and an ESP payload made of a random IV followed by the encrypted data.
tldr.outcome: Any other block cipher can be used with ESP if all the variables described are clearly defined for it.

today: RFC 2451 is a Proposed Standard from November 1998, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is a companion to RFC 2406, which is the ESP specification it refers to.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides confidentiality for IP datagrams by encrypting the payload. RFC 2451 describes how ESP uses CBC-mode cipher algorithms.

It does not cover the default cipher DES, which has its own document (RFC 2405). It is a companion to the ESP specification (RFC 2406) and MUST be read in its context. It assumes familiarity with the IP security architecture (RFC 2401) and the IP security roadmap (RFC 2411).
sections.eli5: ESP is a locked envelope for internet packets. This RFC explains how to use one kind of lock, a chained scrambler, inside that envelope.

sections.title: Common Cipher Variables and CBC Mode
sections.content:
All the symmetric block ciphers share the same variables: mode, key size, weak keys, block size and rounds. The RFC illustrates Blowfish, CAST-128, 3DES, IDEA and RC5, but states that any other block cipher may be used with ESP if all those variables are clearly defined.

Every cipher here uses Cipher Block Chaining (CBC). CBC needs an Initialization Vector (IV) the same size as the block size. The IV is XOR'd with the first plaintext block before encryption. For later blocks, the previous ciphertext block is XOR'd with the current plaintext before encryption. A randomly generated IV prevents identical ciphertext from packets with identical data spanning the first block.
sections.eli5: Each scrambled piece is mixed with the one before it, so the same words never scramble the same way twice. The first piece is mixed with a random starter.

sections.title: Key Sizes, Rounds and Padding
sections.content:
Key sizes MUST be a multiple of 8 bits. The RFC gives a default for each cipher, chosen by consulting experts and balancing strength with performance. The minimum key size for all of the listed ciphers is 40 bits, and the authors strongly advise against anything smaller.

Two notes matter in practice. A CAST-128 key shorter than 128 bits MUST be zero-padded on the right out to 128 bits. For 3DES the three keys come from three consecutive 64-bit pieces, and implementations MUST take the parity bits into account, since each key is really 56 bits plus 8 parity bits.

All of the algorithms use a block size of eight octets (64 bits), and padding must align the data to be encrypted to an eight octet boundary. The number of rounds MAY be negotiated, but a default MUST always exist. For these ciphers rounds are not negotiable: CAST-128 uses 12 rounds for keys up to 80 bits and 16 for longer keys, RC5 16, IDEA 8, Blowfish 16 and 3DES 48 (16x3).
sections.eli5: Longer secret keys are harder to guess, and every cipher chops data into 8-byte chunks, adding filler if needed. Rounds are how many times the scrambling is repeated.

sections.title: Weak Keys and the Ciphers Themselves
sections.content:
Weak key checks SHOULD be performed. A weak key SHOULD be rejected and a new security association requested. The RFC notes that CAST-128 has no known weak keys, RC5 has none known with 16 rounds, IDEA has weak keys, and Blowfish has weak keys that cannot be tested for before the S-box values are generated, though randomly generating one is unlikely.

DES has 64 known weak keys, but for 3DES (DES-EDE3) there is no known need to reject them. However, if the first two or last two 64-bit keys are equal (k1 == k2 or k2 == k3), 3DES is just DES, and implementers MUST reject such keys.

3DES-CBC runs each block through encryption with k1, decryption with k2 and encryption with k3, using the outer chaining technique. If all three keys are equal it is equivalent to DES-CBC, which lets DES-EDE3 hardware work in DES mode. The RFC also gives short backgrounds on each cipher and notes that RC5 is patented and that IDEA is patented in Europe and the United States, with licenses required for commercial use.
sections.eli5: Some secret keys are bad choices, like a lock that opens with almost any key. If you get one, throw it away and pick another.

sections.title: The ESP Payload
sections.content:
The ESP payload is the IV followed by the raw ciphertext. The IV field MUST be the same size as the cipher block, which is 8 octets here, and it MUST be chosen at random. Common practice is random data for the first IV and the last block of encrypted data from the previous encryption as the next IV.

Carrying the IV in every datagram means each datagram can be decrypted even if others are dropped or reordered. Implementations MUST NOT use a counter or other low-Hamming-distance source for IVs, to avoid ECB encryption of very similar plaintext blocks in different packets.

For keying, the key exchange must supply at least as many bits as the key size, and the cipher key is taken from the first bits of the keying material. The RFC knows of no problems between these algorithms and other aspects of ESP.
sections.eli5: Each packet carries its own random starter value, then the scrambled data. So a lost or shuffled packet never stops the others from being read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Implementations are encouraged to use the largest key sizes they can, weighing performance on their hardware and software. Encryption affects both ends of a secure channel, so the cost on the server side counts too. The RFC points to Bellovin's work on the case for random values, and tells readers to consult the documents describing each cipher for further considerations.
sections.eli5: Longer keys are safer but slower for both sides, so choose the longest key your computers can comfortably handle.

viz.caption: ESP PAYLOAD FIELD FOR CBC CIPHERS (RFC 2451)

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: 8 octets, chosen at random, same size as the cipher block.
